nameStory: Field scabious gets its unusual name from an old belief that the plant could cure scabies and other skin conditions - 'scabious' comes from the Latin word for 'scabby' or 'rough.' The 'field' part simply tells us where you're most likely to find it: in open meadows and grassy areas rather than deep in the woods.
description: Field scabious is a medium-sized wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with distinctive pincushion-like flower heads. The pale blue to lavender flowers sit atop long, sturdy stems and have an almost fuzzy appearance due to their many small individual blooms clustered together. This European native has become established in some New England meadows and roadsides, where it blooms through much of the summer. Despite its name suggesting it's weedy, it's actually quite attractive and adds a soft purple hue to wild spaces.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive pincushion-shaped flower heads about 1-2 inches across, with pale blue to lavender color and a slightly fuzzy texture from many tiny individual flowers packed together

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are oval and may be slightly toothed, while upper stem leaves become more deeply divided or lobed, feeling somewhat rough to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 1-3 feet tall with sturdy, upright stems that feel firm and slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Each flower head sits alone at the tip of a long stem, never in clusters, making them look like they're holding court above the foliage

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: After blooming, develops small, dry seed heads that feel papery and contain seeds with tiny bristles that help them stick to clothing and fur

habitat: Look for field scabious in sunny, open areas like meadows, old fields, and roadside verges throughout New England. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun, often growing alongside other European meadow flowers like chicory and Queen Anne's lace. You'll most commonly spot it in areas that were once farmed but have been allowed to return to grassland.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of oval leaves close to the ground, often going unnoticed among other spring growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from June through August, when the distinctive pincushion flowers are most visible and make identification easiest.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and develop into papery seed heads, while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no visible trace above ground until the following spring.

funFact: The flowers are actually made up of dozens of tiny individual blooms packed together, and the outer edge flowers are larger than the inner ones, creating a subtle but beautiful gradient that helps attract butterflies and bees from a distance!
confusionNotes: Field scabious might be confused with wild bergamot or other purple meadow flowers, but its distinctive pincushion shape and pale blue-lavender color set it apart - remember 'pincushion purple' and you'll nail the ID every time.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'field scabious,' this plant is completely unrelated to the Mediterranean scabiosa flowers commonly sold in garden centers - they just happen to share a similar common name due to old medicinal uses.
compareHints: Field scabious is the only Knautia species established in New England, but it's related to teasels in the same plant order. Unlike the spiky, egg-shaped flower heads of wild teasel, field scabious has soft, rounded, pincushion-like blooms. While both are European introductions found in similar habitats, the gentle, fuzzy appearance of field scabious contrasts sharply with teasel's more aggressive, prickly demeanor.
